32 — Monitoring and Observability Checklist#

Verify that critical services and user journeys can be understood through trustworthy telemetry, actionable alerts, service-level measurements, and effective incident investigation. Monitoring systems must also be reliable, proportionate, and privacy-conscious.

Scope: Backend / API-specific. This file is one part of the 32_Monitoring_and_Observability.md checklist. Apply the domain-wide release gate across all applicable scope files; each checklist ID remains unique.

Review details#

  • Project / product:
  • Release / version / environment:
  • Scope and applicable jurisdictions / markets:
  • Critical services / user journeys:
  • Monitoring and incident-response owners:
  • SLI / SLO / alerting policy reference:
  • Reviewer / owner:
  • Review date:
  • Decision: Pending / Approved / Approved with documented exceptions / Blocked

How to use#

  1. Copy the shared template into project-specific review records; leave all checkboxes in this repository unchecked.
  2. Mark [x] only after verifying the item through instrumentation configuration, actual dashboards and queries, sample logs/traces, controlled alert tests, incident drills, or other documented evidence. Record failed checks and N/A reasons in project-specific notes or issue tracking keyed by OBS ID.
  3. Identify user-critical journeys and their real failure modes before selecting metrics, alert thresholds, or telemetry vendors. Adjust monitoring depth to expected operational risk and staff coverage.
  4. Review ## API Checks and ## Frontend Checks separately when relevant; record genuinely inapplicable checks outside the shared template.
  5. Reassess instrumentation and alerts after deployments, new data flows, new critical features, incidents, and changes to support arrangements. Monitoring review is not a substitute for separate Security, Privacy, Reliability, or Performance reviews.

Telemetry and instrumentation#

  • OBS-001 Inventory the critical services, infrastructure, data pipelines, background jobs, and user journeys that require observability.
  • OBS-002 Assign an accountable owner to the telemetry produced by each service and to its collection and storage pipeline.
  • OBS-005 Use stable service, environment, version, and deployment identifiers to support filtering and release comparisons.
  • OBS-011 Instrument database, cache, message queue, storage, and third-party calls where they materially affect critical workflows.
  • OBS-012 Capture background-job start, completion, failure, retry, and queue-lag signals where asynchronous work is used.
  • OBS-013 Measure resource utilization and saturation for compute, memory, disk, connections, and other constrained pools.
  • OBS-014 Choose metric labels with controlled cardinality; avoid unbounded user, request, URL, or document identifiers as dimensions.
  • OBS-016 Verify telemetry timestamps, time zones, and clock synchronization are sufficient for cross-service investigations.
  • OBS-018 Review automatic instrumentation and telemetry schemas for accidental capture of personal data, tokens, credentials, or sensitive request content.
  • OBS-019 Configure filtering, redaction, or attribute allowlists before sensitive telemetry enters broadly accessible stores where feasible.
  • OBS-020 Secure telemetry ingestion, exports, and collectors with authenticated transport and appropriate privilege boundaries.
  • OBS-022 Test telemetry pipeline behavior during backend unavailability, queue saturation, restart, and recovery, including acceptable data-loss assumptions.
  • OBS-024 Confirm deployed services emit the expected signals in the actual production environment before treating monitoring as complete.
  • OBS-006 Publish structured application logs with consistent timestamps, severity levels, event names, and correlation fields.
  • OBS-007 Include enough context in error logs to investigate failures without dumping entire payloads or secrets.
  • OBS-008 Propagate trace context across synchronous service boundaries and compatible asynchronous message flows where appropriate.
  • OBS-009 Create spans around critical work and downstream calls, identifying bottlenecks and failures without excessive instrumentation.
  • OBS-010 Correlate logs with traces through valid trace or span identifiers when supported by the chosen stack.
  • OBS-015 Choose trace sampling and metric aggregation that preserve meaningful error and tail-latency visibility within cost limits.
  • OBS-021 Monitor collector ingestion, processing failures, queues, export errors, and dropped or delayed data as first-class reliability signals.
  • OBS-023 Keep instrumentation, collector configuration, and dashboard queries under reviewable version control where supported.

Alerting and on-call#

  • OBS-026 Page primarily on actionable symptoms of user impact rather than every infrastructure event or transient cause.
  • OBS-037 Alert when a critical monitoring target disappears or the telemetry pipeline stops delivering expected data.
  • OBS-038 Distinguish missing or stale telemetry from a healthy zero value in relevant alerts and dashboards.

Service-level indicators and objectives#

  • OBS-047 Select indicators that reflect actual user experience instead of relying only on server or instance uptime.
  • OBS-048 Measure successful and failed request latency separately where error responses could distort normal latency distributions.
  • OBS-053 Use synthetic or external probes for critical endpoints or journeys when internal telemetry could miss a total outage.
  • OBS-056 Evaluate multi-window or burn-rate alerts for SLO exhaustion where request volume supports reliable calculations.
  • OBS-058 Validate monitoring queries and dashboard aggregations against known examples, raw samples, or controlled failures.

Incident investigation and learning#

  • OBS-066 Correlate deploys, configuration changes, infrastructure events, and feature-flag updates with changing service health.
  • OBS-067 Provide reliable access to production observability for authorized responders, including suitable emergency access procedures.

API Checks#

  • OBS-082 Instrument each critical API route or operation with request rate, latency distributions, and error counts.
  • OBS-083 Distinguish server failures, expected client errors, authentication failures, and throttling in API dashboards.
  • OBS-084 Tag operations using stable route templates or endpoint identifiers instead of raw, high-cardinality URL paths.
  • OBS-085 Capture service version, deployment environment, and dependency identity to support regression investigations.
  • OBS-086 Propagate trace context through API gateways, application handlers, downstream calls, and compatible message consumers.
  • OBS-087 Correlate a safe request identifier between API error responses, server logs, and tracing where appropriate.
  • OBS-088 Record upstream and downstream dependency latency, failures, retries, timeouts, and circuit-breaker events.
  • OBS-089 Monitor database-query and connection-pool metrics when API performance or reliability depends on them.
  • OBS-090 Observe async API jobs, queues, webhook delivery, consumer lag, and dead-letter volume where applicable.
  • OBS-091 Capture API authorization and security-relevant events through access-controlled logs without disclosing credentials or sensitive payloads.
  • OBS-092 Use rate-limit and quota metrics to distinguish intended throttling from widespread overload or abuse.
  • OBS-093 Monitor request and response size distributions where payload growth could impair availability.
  • OBS-094 Test that long-running streams and bidirectional protocols emit meaningful connection, cancellation, and failure signals.
  • OBS-095 Make SLI queries distinguish critical routes and consumer groups without excessive label cardinality.
  • OBS-096 Verify telemetry for API validation, not-found, conflict, and degraded-dependency outcomes is interpretable.
  • OBS-097 Check API traces and logs during a staged failure or controlled test to confirm correct causal relationships.
  • OBS-098 Document expected status codes and failure semantics before defining alert rules to avoid paging on normal behavior.
  • OBS-099 Keep API instrumentation overhead bounded and confirm failure of exporters does not disable core requests.
  • OBS-100 Ensure outbound telemetry strips secrets and personal fields that may appear in headers, query strings, and bodies.

Release gate#

  • Critical user journeys and dependent services have identifiable monitoring owners, useful health indicators, and working observability access.
  • Service-level objectives or other accepted reliability expectations have clearly defined measurement and incident-detection methods where applicable.
  • Meaningful user-impact alerts reach appropriate responders; alert routing, escalation, and at least one representative trigger have been tested.
  • Logs, metrics, traces, and dashboard views needed to investigate a critical failure are usable, correlated where necessary, and tagged with the deployed version or environment.
  • Telemetry pipelines report their own health or absence of data, and logging/monitoring does not expose prohibited sensitive information.
  • API and frontend error, latency, and critical-journey indicators are reviewed where those interfaces exist, including known collection and sampling limits.
  • Incident response roles, escalation procedures, relevant runbooks, and unresolved observability gaps have accountable owners and authorized dispositions in project-specific records.

Domain-specific approval rule: Block monitoring sign-off if a critical user-impacting failure cannot reasonably be detected or investigated, required alerts do not reach responders, monitoring is materially blind without accepted mitigation, or sensitive telemetry exposure remains unresolved. Dashboard existence alone does not establish production observability.

Trusted references and scope#

These checks translate authoritative observability and operations guidance into practical verification tasks. They do not mandate a specific vendor, instrumentation SDK, or SLO target.

  • OpenTelemetry — Signals — core telemetry concepts and selecting logs, metrics, and traces.
  • OpenTelemetry — Semantic conventions — consistent operation, resource, metric, log, and trace attributes.
  • OpenTelemetry — Logs — structured logging, stable schema, and correlation.
  • OpenTelemetry — Handling sensitive data — data minimization, redaction, and telemetry privacy.
  • OpenTelemetry — Collector resiliency — telemetry queueing, exporter failures, and data-loss controls.
  • Google SRE — Monitoring Distributed Systems — four golden signals and symptom-driven monitoring.
  • Google SRE Workbook — Monitoring — service and dependency signals and operational dashboards.
  • Google SRE Workbook — Alerting on SLOs — error-budget and multi-window burn-rate alerting.
  • Google SRE Workbook — Postmortem Culture — blameless incident learning and follow-up ownership.
  • Prometheus — Alerting best practices — actionable, user-impact-focused alerts and monitoring of monitoring.
  • Prometheus — Alerting rules — alerting thresholds, pending durations, labels, and annotations.
  • Grafana — Alerting best practices — routing, severity, useful alerts, and alert noise management.
  • web.dev — Web Vitals — client-side loading, interactivity, and layout stability metrics.

Applicability: Monitoring requirements depend on the service's criticality, traffic, architecture, user population, jurisdiction, and available operational coverage. Tracing across distributed services, browser Web Vitals, SLO burn-rate paging, and OpenTelemetry Collector configuration are conditional, not universal. Sample size and low-traffic behavior must be considered before configuring percentage-based alerts. Keep sensitive personal, financial, health, and credential data out of broadly visible telemetry.

Source review date: 2026-11-12.

Suggested testing tools#

Choose tools appropriate to the project's stack and risks; automation supports evidence but does not approve the checklist.

  • Test focus: trace propagation, metrics/logs, alert conditions, and SLO visibility; include API and service behavior where applicable.
  • Cross-stack: Prometheus promtool + OpenTelemetry.
  • Python: OpenTelemetry + pytest; for pytest-based suites, run python -m pytest -q.
  • TypeScript: OpenTelemetry + Vitest; for Vitest-based suites, run npx vitest run (or npx playwright test for E2E).
  • JavaScript: OpenTelemetry + Jest; for Jest-based suites, run npx jest --ci (or npx playwright test for E2E).
  • Evidence: Save tool versions, configuration, test environment, fixtures, results, and links in project-specific review records using the existing checklist IDs. Expert review remains necessary where relevant.

Suggested AI skills for verification#

These are optional agent review aids, not automated passes or release approval. Each linked repository had at least 1,000 GitHub stars when checked on 2026-11-12; counts are per repository, not per skill, and do not indicate security or correctness.

  • observability-and-instrumentation — Check telemetry and diagnosis coverage (addyosmani/agent-skills, 116,378 repo stars).
  • distributed-tracing — Check tracing across service boundaries (wshobson/agents, 42,437 repo stars).
  • slo-implementation — Review alerting and objective measurements (wshobson/agents, 42,437 repo stars).

How to check: In a project-specific copy, have the agent audit the backend / API scope and map findings to this file's existing checklist IDs, with code/configuration references, reproducible test results, failed or inapplicable cases, and uncertainties. Independently verify findings; keep shared template boxes unchecked and retain human approval requirements.

Before use: Read the skill's SKILL.md, referenced scripts, license, and requested tool permissions. Only execute vetted skills with appropriate access in a controlled environment.

Important warning: reference only#

⚠️ Reference only — not a definitive or exhaustive checklist. This template is a starting point for review, not the ultimate authority or a guarantee of project safety, quality, regulatory compliance, accessibility, security, or launch readiness.

Use project-specific judgment and independent verification. Requirements and risks evolve and differ by project, technology, and jurisdiction. Adapt the checks, consult current authoritative sources, perform relevant tests, and obtain qualified specialist review or approval when appropriate. Checking every box does not replace these steps.

Reference, not a certification. Check applicability, verify important claims against current primary sources, and seek expert review where necessary. Suggest an improvement.
